title: Letter and Witness
premise: Kestrel Vane, a night-shift taxi dispatcher with a gift for hearing what callers don't say, has quietly unraveled three deaths the police ruled accidental. When a missing woman's diary arrives at the dispatch office—entries continuing weeks past her disappearance—Kestrel realizes the woman may be alive, hiding, and leaving a coded trail through the company's own fare ledgers. As a corrupt detective closes in and the statute of limitations on the original crime expires, Kestrel must choose between protecting the person she's grown to love and exposing a justice system that buried the truth. In the end, Kestrel decodes the ledger, confronts the killer on the last night before the deadline, and delivers the evidence not to the police but to a journalist—choosing truth over loyalty, and finding that love survives the choice.
about_author: Petra Sterling is the pen name of a former emergency dispatcher who spent eleven years listening to a city breathe through a headset before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries from a converted garage in the Pacific Northwest, where she still keeps her old dispatch logs for inspiration.

chapters.title: The Night Frequency
chapters.summary: Kestrel Vane works the graveyard shift at Meridian Taxi, dispatching cabs and cataloging the city's secrets in a private notebook. A routine call from a frightened woman named Ada Lorne ends abruptly mid-sentence. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: quiet competence shadowed by unease—the listener senses something wrong in the static.

chapters.title: Three Accidents
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter revealing how Kestrel solved three prior deaths the police called accidents, using fare records, call audio, and pattern recognition—all anonymously, via typed letters. Her only confidant is Marcus, an aging driver who owes her his life. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: pride tangled with isolation; invisibility as both armor and prison.

chapters.title: Ada Lorne, Missing
chapters.summary: Ada is reported missing; police find no body, no struggle, and quickly lose interest. Kestrel replays the dispatch tape and hears a second voice in the background—a man counting money. She files it away, telling herself it isn't her problem. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: guilt curdling into resolve.

chapters.title: The Package
chapters.summary: A padded envelope arrives at the dispatch office containing Ada's diary—postmarked three weeks after her disappearance. The final entry is dated tomorrow. Kestrel realizes someone wants her to find it, or wants her implicated. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: dread and exhilaration colliding; the game has found her.

chapters.title: Detective Rook
chapters.summary: Detective Elias Rook, who dismissed all three of Kestrel's anonymous letters, appears at the dispatch office asking about Ada—and about 'the letter writer.' His interest feels predatory rather than procedural. POV: alternating Kestrel and Rook. Emotional beat: cat-and-mouse tension; the hunter suspects the invisible hand.

chapters.title: Ledger Lines
chapters.summary: Kestrel notices the diary's dates correspond to fare numbers in Meridian's old paper ledgers—Ada was a bookkeeper here before vanishing. Certain entries are written in a numeric cipher keyed to cab routes. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: the thrill of the puzzle rekindled; the city becomes a text to be read.

chapters.title: Marcus Knows Something
chapters.summary: Marcus grows evasive when Kestrel asks about the year Ada worked at Meridian. She discovers he drove the route that matches the diary's first cipher entry the night Ada disappeared. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: loyalty tested; the first crack in the one relationship she trusts.

chapters.title: Route 9 After Midnight
chapters.summary: Following the decoded route, Kestrel finds a storage unit rented under a dead man's name. Inside: financial records showing Meridian's owner, Dale Pruitt, laundering money through fares—with Ada's annotations flagging the largest sums. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: vertigo; the small mystery opens onto something much larger.

chapters.title: What the Diary Doesn't Say
chapters.summary: Rook confronts Kestrel privately, revealing he knows she wrote the letters—but instead of arresting her, he offers a deal: help him nail Pruitt, and he'll bury her involvement. Kestrel doesn't trust him. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: cornered calculation; every ally might be a trap.

chapters.title: The Statute Clock
chapters.summary: Kestrel learns the statute of limitations on the underlying fraud expires in eleven days—after which the ledger evidence becomes legally worthless. Whoever sent the diary chose this window deliberately. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: urgency compresses everything; the story becomes a countdown.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Kestrel and Rook work uneasy nights together decoding entries, and an unexpected tenderness grows between them—complicated by her certainty that Rook is hiding his own connection to Pruitt. POV: alternating. Emotional beat: warmth blooming in hostile ground; trust as a risk taken, not given.

chapters.title: The Dead Man's Fare
chapters.summary: Decoded entry seven points to a hit-and-run two years ago that Kestrel's first anonymous letter had flagged. The victim was an auditor. Ada didn't just witness fraud—she witnessed murder, and ran. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: horror deepening; the stakes shift from exposure to survival.

chapters.title: Someone Is Driving My Cab
chapters.summary: Kestrel's apartment is searched while she's on shift. Nothing is stolen except her copy of the diary pages. Only Marcus knew where she kept them. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: betrayal's cold shock; paranoia replaces every comfortable assumption.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Garage
chapters.summary: Kestrel corners Marcus. He confesses: years ago Pruitt bought his silence after the auditor's death, and Marcus recognized Ada's handwriting in the diary—he took the pages to protect Kestrel from the same fate. POV: Marcus, then Kestrel. Emotional beat: grief and forgiveness entangled; loyalty revealed as both sin and salvation.

chapters.title: Pruitt's Invitation
chapters.summary: Dale Pruitt invites Kestrel to dinner, all charm, making clear he knows exactly who she is and offering her a job—and a warning. He mentions Ada in the past tense. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: controlled terror under a civil mask; evil wearing a friendly face.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Kestrel cracks the final cipher: the last diary entry encodes coordinates and a date—the night before the statute expires. Ada planned to surface then, with everything. Which means Pruitt knows the deadline too, and will be there. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: terrible clarity; the trap is set for both hunter and prey.

chapters.title: Rook's Confession
chapters.summary: Rook admits he once took money from Pruitt early in his career—the case he could never close is the case that owns him. Helping Kestrel is his redemption or his ruin. They become true partners. POV: Rook. Emotional beat: shame transmuted into purpose; duty reclaimed through confession.

chapters.title: Vanishing Point
chapters.summary: On the appointed night, Kestrel and Rook stake out the coordinates—an abandoned ferry terminal. Pruitt's men arrive first. Then a figure steps from the dark: Ada Lorne, alive, carrying the original ledger. Shots are fired. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: adrenaline and awe; the impossible made flesh.

chapters.title: Terminal Velocity
chapters.summary: Climax: a chase through the terminal as Pruitt tries to burn the ledger and take Ada with it. Marcus arrives in his cab as getaway and shield. Rook takes a bullet protecting the evidence. Kestrel subdues Pruitt using the same listening skills that started it all—she heard the ambush coming. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: courage crystallized; the invisible woman fully seen.

chapters.title: Letter, Not Witness
chapters.summary: With Rook hospitalized and Pruitt arrested, Kestrel faces a choice: testify and become a public figure, or hand everything to investigative journalist Rena Okafor and disappear again. She chooses the journalist—justice outside the courtroom, truth without the spotlight. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: bittersweet self-knowledge; some invisibility is chosen, not imposed.

chapters.title: Ada's Fare
chapters.summary: Ada, recovering and free, thanks Kestrel and reveals why she chose her: the dispatch tapes showed Kestrel was the only one who ever really listened. The two women form a quiet alliance. Marcus retires; Rook, healing, asks Kestrel to dinner—not as a detective. POV: Ada, then Kestrel. Emotional beat: tenderness earned; love allowed to exist beside duty rather than against it.

chapters.title: Night Shift, New Frequency
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Kestrel returns to the dispatch desk, the city's voices flowing through her headset. A frightened caller hesitates on the line—and Kestrel, wiser now, doesn't stay invisible. She picks up the phone herself. POV: Kestrel. Emotional beat: resolution and renewal; the listener becomes the voice, and the night shift finally feels like home.
